lesson.title: Anatomy of a Thought: The Building Blocks of the Nervous System
lesson.summary: Neurons are the specialized cells that receive, integrate, and transmit electrochemical signals, and their four main parts, dendrites, cell body, axon, and terminal buttons, each serve a distinct step in moving information along.
lesson.body:
Every thought, sensation, and movement described so far depends on a single kind of cell: the neuron. Neurons are the basic functional units of the nervous system, and the brain and spinal cord that make up the central nervous system are built from billions of them, wired together into circuits of staggering complexity. A typical neuron has four main structural regions, and the shape of each region reflects the specific job it does in moving information along. Not every neuron looks identical: most interneurons are multipolar, with many dendrites branching from the cell body, while many sensory neurons have a distinctive shape in which a single process leaves the cell body and splits into two branches, one reaching toward the periphery and one toward the spinal cord. Despite these variations, the same basic dendrite, cell body, axon, and terminal button plan applies across nearly all of them.

The first region is the dendrites, branch-like extensions that reach out from the cell body to receive incoming signals from other neurons. Because dendrites are often numerous and highly branched, a single neuron can receive input from thousands of other neurons at once, giving it the raw material to combine many small signals into one decision about whether to fire.

Those signals arrive at the cell body, or soma, which contains the nucleus and the cellular machinery that keeps the neuron alive, and which also serves as the integration point where incoming signals are summed together. If the combined input crosses a critical threshold, the cell body triggers an electrical signal that travels down the next structure, the axon, a single long fiber that carries the signal away from the cell body toward other neurons, muscles, or glands.

Many axons are wrapped in a fatty layer called the myelin sheath, produced by glial cells, which insulates the axon and dramatically speeds up signal transmission by allowing the electrical impulse to jump between small gaps in the sheath rather than travel continuously along the entire length. Axons vary enormously in length: some interneurons connect to their neighbors over a fraction of a millimeter, while a single motor neuron axon can run from the spinal cord all the way down to a muscle in the foot.

At the very end of the axon are the terminal buttons, also called axon terminals, which release chemical messengers called neurotransmitters into the tiny gap, or synapse, between one neuron and the next. This is where an electrical signal within one neuron becomes a chemical signal capable of influencing the next cell in the chain. Picture a sensory neuron in your fingertip: its dendrites detect pressure, its cell body integrates that input, its axon carries the resulting signal all the way up to your spinal cord, and its terminal buttons release neurotransmitters onto the next neuron in the circuit, continuing the message toward your brain. This one-directional flow, receiving through dendrites, integrating in the cell body, and sending through the axon, is what allows information in the nervous system to move along consistent, organized pathways rather than spreading randomly in every direction.
